To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the four Orders of Outcome framework and the ICM policy cycle are useful frameworks for: (a) organizing and assessing the outcomes of ICM initiatives and their constituent projects and programs; and (b) organizing and assessing progress and learning in portfolios of ICM projects and programs.

(1) the ICM Policy Cycle and the Orders of Outcomes frameworks can be applied to a wide variety of ICM initiatives; (2) the application of these frameworks has revealed that the outcomes of ICM initiatives are not always what was expected, and (3) the frameworks can help ICM practitioners and researchers to understand why this occurs and to improve the effectiveness of ICM initiatives.
ICM initiatives are complex, dynamic, adaptive processes that can lead to improved coastal development and conservation outcomes if they are given sufficient time to evolve.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What are the critical elements of the ICM process that lead to sustainable outcomes?
the evolution of ICS initiatives over extended time periods.
understanding the dynamics of ICM as a process and the conditions under which it is likely to be sustained.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the framework and indicators are a powerful and useful tool for assessing progress in ICM initiatives.
there is a need for more and more comprehensive ICM.

there is a need for an ICM assessment framework that is: (1) simple enough to be understood and used by all stakeholders, (2) comprehensive enough to capture the complexity of the issues and the diversity of the ICM initiatives, (3) flexible enough to accommodate the variety of governance structures and (4) dynamic enough to capture the evolution of the ICM initiative over time.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the frameworks are useful in helping us to think more clearly about what we are trying to accomplish in the coastal arena and to assess progress in achieving our goals.
the more we learn about the nature of the ICM problem, the more we realize that it is an extremely challenging problem to solve.
ICM is not a panacea, but it does offer a promising framework for achieving more sustainable forms of development.
The main takeaway from our work is that

ICM is a learning process that is best assessed by the progress that is being made in the four Orders of Outcome and the ICM policy cycle, rather than by the more traditional measures of outputs, outcomes and impacts that are used to assess the performance of projects and programs in other sectors.
ICM initiatives are more likely to be successful if they are designed with a clear sense of the desired end states and the sequence of intermediate steps that will be required to reach them.
ICM initiatives are complex, long-term processes that are best viewed as a series of steps that are linked in a logical sequence.
